big_idea: Negotiation is not a rational exchange of information but an emotional, psychological process. The negotiator who best understands and manages the other side's emotions, rather than splitting the difference, wins better outcomes for everyone.

tool.label: Tactical empathy: mirroring and labeling
tool.text: Mirroring means repeating the last one to three words your counterpart just said, then staying silent, which prompts them to elaborate; labeling means naming their emotion aloud, it seems like or it sounds like, to validate the feeling without agreeing to their position, which lowers defensiveness.
tool.note: Voss developed these as an FBI international hostage negotiator and adapted them for business and everyday negotiations.

ideas.title: Calibrated questions
ideas.text: Open-ended what and how questions give the other side the illusion of control while steering the outcome your way.

ideas.title: That's right vs. you're right
ideas.text: The goal is to summarize the other person's position so well they say that's right, a sign of real breakthrough; you're right usually just means they want you to stop talking.

ideas.title: The accusation audit
ideas.text: List every negative thing the other party could say about you and say it first, disarming their objections before they raise them.

ideas.title: Black swans
ideas.text: Every negotiation holds hidden, unknown information that, once surfaced through careful listening, can flip the deal in your favor.

ideas.title: The Ackerman model
ideas.text: A structured concession pattern, roughly 65%, 85%, 95%, then 100% of your target, using non-round numbers to make final offers feel more credible.

ideas.title: No-oriented questions
ideas.text: Asking questions that make it easy for the other side to say no reduces their defensiveness and opens dialogue.

try_it: In your next tense conversation, mirror the last three words someone says and pause; notice how much more they explain.
Try labeling an emotion you observe in someone instead of arguing with their position.
Before a request or ask this week, run your own accusation audit: write down what the other person might think is unfair about it, and name it upfront.
Practice a calibrated how question instead of a direct demand.
best_for: People negotiating salary, deals, or high-stakes asks
Managers and salespeople wanting concrete verbal scripts
less_useful: Readers looking for cooperative, win-win negotiation theory, since it leans persuasive and somewhat adversarial
Those wanting academic rigor over FBI-style anecdote

related.why: A similarly frame-driven approach to controlling a high-stakes interaction
The bigger picture of the emotional escalation these tactics are designed to interrupt
